findings.title: Async legacy writes inherit a request context that is canceled on response completion
findings.body: The timeout context is derived from the request context captured by the handler. For normal HTTP/API-server requests that parent context is canceled when the handler returns, while this work is deliberately still running asynchronously. Consequently Legacy.Create can be canceled before or during its write even though the caller has already received a successful unified-storage response; the same issue exists in the Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection goroutines at lines 110, 135, and 163. Use a writer-owned background context (while preserving required values) with its own timeout and shutdown lifecycle rather than the request cancellation context.

findings.title: Independent async mirror writes do not preserve write ordering
findings.body: Every successful unified write starts an independent goroutine, with no per-resource serialization or sequencing. For example, a unified delete followed by a create of the same name can run in the opposite order in legacy storage: the create completes first and the delayed delete then removes the newly created object. Consecutive updates can similarly leave an older version as the final legacy state. This makes the legacy copy diverge permanently; queue or serialize mirror operations by resource, or apply a monotonic version/sequence check.

findings.title: Legacy update re-evaluates the original update callback instead of mirroring the unified result
findings.body: Storage.Update has already evaluated objInfo against the unified store's old object before this goroutine starts, but Legacy.Update is given the original objInfo and will evaluate UpdatedObject again against a potentially stale or different legacy object. UpdatedObjectInfo is explicitly old-object dependent and can perform transformations or have side effects, so the two stores can receive different payloads. The prior implementation materialized the update and wrapped the unified result for the legacy write; retain an immutable materialized result for the asynchronous mirror operation.

findings.title: A unified NotFound delete no longer attempts legacy cleanup
findings.body: This early return covers NotFound errors, so a resource that exists only in legacy storage is left there when it is deleted through mode 3. The previous implementation explicitly continued to Legacy.Delete for a unified NotFound while returning the unified error to the caller. Leaving the stale legacy object visible through legacy APIs also risks resurrecting it if the migration is rolled back; preserve the NotFound cleanup path, asynchronously if needed.

findings.title: Delete metrics use resource names as the kind label
findings.body: recordStorageDuration's third argument is the resource kind everywhere else, but this call supplies the user-controlled object name. This both misclassifies delete metrics and creates a distinct Prometheus histogram series for every deleted object name, causing unbounded metric cardinality and potentially substantial memory/scrape overhead. Pass options.Kind instead.

findings.title: Legacy replication has no concurrency or queue bound
findings.body: A goroutine is spawned for every successful write, and each can remain active for up to ten seconds (or longer if a legacy implementation does not honor context cancellation). A slow or unavailable legacy backend therefore lets normal unified writes accumulate an unbounded number of goroutines and backend connections with no backpressure, risking process resource exhaustion under write load. Use a bounded worker pool/queue and define behavior when it is full.

findings.title: Duration metrics are attributed to the wrong storage backend
findings.body: A Storage.Create failure is recorded through recordLegacyDuration even though no legacy call was made; the same mistake occurs for Storage.Update at line 129. Conversely, the async Legacy.DeleteCollection call at line 166 is recorded with recordStorageDuration after storage was already recorded at line 159. This produces false backend latency/error rates and can hide primary-storage failures during the migration rollout.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not verify that the asynchronous legacy write occurs
findings.body: Both storage wrappers share the same mock.Mock, their expectations have identical method signatures, and the tests never call AssertExpectations or wait for the goroutine. Thus the synchronous unified call can satisfy the configured method pattern and a regression that never invokes Legacy.Create/Delete/Update/DeleteCollection would still pass. Use distinct backend mocks plus a channel/eventual assertion to verify exactly one legacy call after successful unified writes and no legacy call after primary failures.

findings.title: The mode 3 integration test assumes an asynchronous legacy mirror is immediately visible
findings.body: The newly added mode 3 subtests execute doPlaylistTests, which performs K8s writes and then immediately requires the legacy playlist list to contain those objects at this assertion (with similar immediate legacy reads later). Mode 3 intentionally returns before the legacy write completes, so scheduler or CI load can make these assertions fail nondeterministically. Poll for eventual legacy consistency with a bounded timeout, or otherwise synchronize the test with the mirror operation.
